standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Adult life-skills: self-knowledge, decisions, transitions & support (UNESCO 5.2, 5.6, 5.1, 5.5). New v2 build, Chapter 5 (penultimate, before Decoded). You're about to run your own life: know yourself and your values, decide well, handle the big stuff (board exams, leaving home, failure, uncertainty), work with people, and build a support network you can lean on, for good. The culmination of the feelings-and-life-skills thread (Feelings Friends -> Heart Smart -> Mind Matters -> Bounce -> Life Ready), consolidating the Life-Skills Toolkit for adult life. Builds on g39 (Bounce); draws on g16 (Crossroads); precedes g36. Healthy strategies only (never pain/shock/self-destructive); pressure-free decisions (no single 'right' life path beyond safety & law); help-seeking is a lifelong strength, not a failure; NOT therapy. India: board-exam pressure, family/career expectations, the transition to college/work; routes distress to Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN 1800-599-0019, Manodarpan, a trusted adult/mentor.
evidenceBase: Good adult decisions start with self-knowledge: your values, strengths and what matters to you, plus emotional self-awareness. There are no 'right' values, only the work of knowing your own; and mature decision-making is a learnable method, gather the facts, weigh them against your values and goals, think through consequences and the long term, resist pressure, choose and own it, with no single 'right' answer beyond safety and the law (UNESCO KC5; WHO life skills)

Late adolescence brings big, real transitions and stress (board exams and results, leaving home, new independence, relationships changing, failure, uncertainty); in India around 81% of students cite schoolwork and exams as a source of anxiety. These are met with healthy strategies only, name the stress, use a healthy coping tool, break it down, lean on your people, and ask for help early, never pain, shock or self-destructive coping; failure is an event to learn from, not an identity, and change is hard and survivable (WHO adolescent mental health; NCERT Manodarpan survey)

Half of adult life is other people (clear communication, listening, collaboration, boundaries, resolving conflict), and the thread's most important message is that you don't have to do adulthood alone: build a support network (friends, family, a mentor or teacher, a counsellor or professional), because help-seeking continues for life rather than ending at 18 and is a strength, not a failure. This is life-skills education, not therapy, and it routes serious or persistent distress to real support, Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN 1800-599-0019, Manodarpan, or a trusted adult (MoE Manodarpan; WHO)

scenarios.hook: Lensy: good adult decisions start with knowing yourself, your values and what matters. Ready to map that?
scenarios.affirm: Self-knowledge is the base every good decision is built on, you're starting in the right place.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your values and what matters is the base of good decisions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what matters most to you as you head into adult life?
scenarios.affirm: Naming what matters to you is the start of living by it, whatever you chose.
scenarios.relearn: Naming what matters to you is the start of living by your values.

scenarios.hook: "There's a set of 'right' values you're supposed to have."

myth.un: There's a 'right' set of values you must have.
myth.re: There are no 'right' values to copy; the work is knowing your own.
myth.why: Self-knowledge is personal, not a template.

scenarios.relearn: There's no 'right' set of values; the work is knowing your own.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds self-awareness, or avoids it?

items.text: Noticing how you actually feel and react
Reflecting on what matters to you

scenarios.relearn: Noticing your feelings and reflecting builds self-awareness; pretending and just-conforming avoid it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing your strengths is as important as knowing your values. What's one of yours?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing a real strength of yours is something to build your future on.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your strengths gives you something to build on.

scenarios.hook: You're about to make choices that should fit who you are, but you've never thought about your values.

options.text: Take time to figure out your values first
options.consequence: Your choices start lining up with who you are.

options.text: Just decide on impulse
options.consequence: Knowing your values first makes choices fit you; impulse alone often doesn't.

scenarios.debrief: A little self-reflection makes every choice that follows truer to you.
scenarios.relearn: Figure out your values first; choices then fit who you are.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what do you want your life to stand for?
scenarios.affirm: A sense of what you want to stand for is a compass for the years ahead.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing what you want your life to stand for is a compass.

scenarios.hook: "By now you should have your whole self and future figured out."

myth.un: By now you should have yourself and your future all figured out.
myth.re: Self-knowledge unfolds for life; you only need to start, not finish.
myth.why: No one has it all worked out, at any age.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need yourself all figured out; self-knowledge unfolds for life.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to know yourself, or a trap?
scenarios.relearn: Kind, honest reflection builds self-knowledge; harsh self-criticism and comparison don't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: emotional self-awareness, noticing how you feel and why, helps you handle whatever comes. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Noticing your feelings and their causes is the start of handling them well.
scenarios.relearn: Emotional self-awareness helps you handle whatever comes.

scenarios.hook: Match the self-knowledge to what it guides.
scenarios.relearn: Values guide decisions, strengths guide building, feelings guide coping.

scenarios.hook: Others have strong opinions about who you should be.

options.text: Listen, but decide who you are by your own reflection
options.consequence: You stay the author of your own identity.

options.text: Become whoever they want
options.consequence: Listen to others, but author your own identity by your own values.

scenarios.debrief: Input from others is useful; the final word on who you are is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Hear others, but decide who you are by your own values.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a private 'values map' you carry, does that feel like a useful thing to have?
scenarios.affirm: A values map is a quiet compass you can return to whenever a choice is hard.
scenarios.relearn: A personal values map is a compass for hard choices.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing yourself isn't about being perfect, it's about being honest with yourself. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Honesty with yourself, not perfection, is what real self-knowledge is.
scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge is honesty with yourself, not perfection.

scenarios.hook: You face a big decision about study or your future. How do you approach it?

options.text: Gather facts, weigh your values and the long term, then choose and own it
options.consequence: You make a real, considered, self-owned decision.

options.text: Go with whatever feels easiest right now
options.consequence: The adult method, facts, values, long term, then own it, beats easiest-now.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding like an adult: facts, values, consequences, the long game, then own it.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by facts, values and the long term, then own the choice.

scenarios.hook: Match the decision step to what it does.
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values and the long term are the core of a good decision.

scenarios.hook: "There's one right life path and you must find it."

myth.un: There's one right life path you have to find.
myth.re: There's no single 'right' path; the skill is deciding well by your own values.
myth.why: Many good lives are possible; deciding well is what counts.

scenarios.relearn: There's no single right path; decide well by your own values.

scenarios.hook: Family and friends are pushing you toward different choices.

options.text: Weigh their input, then decide by your own values and goals
options.consequence: You make a choice you can stand behind.

options.text: Pick whoever pushes hardest
options.consequence: Weigh others' input, but decide by your own values, not who pushes hardest.

scenarios.debrief: Others' input informs you; your values make the final call.
scenarios.relearn: Weigh others' input, but decide by your own values and goals.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a good basis for a big decision, or a poor one?
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values and consequences are a good basis; panic and image aren't.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to rush a big choice to get it over with.

options.text: Take the time a real decision needs
options.consequence: You decide well rather than fast.

options.text: Rush it to stop the discomfort
options.consequence: Big decisions deserve the time they need; don't rush to escape discomfort.

scenarios.debrief: Important decisions are worth slowing down for.
scenarios.relearn: Take the time a big decision needs; don't rush it.

scenarios.hook: A decision involves money basics for the first time.

options.text: Get the facts and think about needs vs wants and the future
options.consequence: You make a sensible, informed money choice.

options.text: Spend on impulse and hope
options.consequence: For money, get the facts and weigh needs, wants and the future.

scenarios.debrief: Money decisions use the same method: facts, values, long term.
scenarios.relearn: For money choices, weigh facts, needs vs wants, and the future.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'owning' a decision means you chose it and you'll see it through. Feel the difference from drifting?
scenarios.affirm: Owning your choices, rather than drifting into them, is what adult agency feels like.
scenarios.relearn: Owning a decision means you chose it and will see it through.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of the adult decision method, or not?
scenarios.relearn: Facts and values are in the method; ignoring consequences and deferring entirely aren't.

scenarios.hook: "A good decision is one that turns out perfectly."

myth.un: A good decision is one that turns out perfectly.
myth.re: A good decision is one made well, with the facts and values you had; outcomes aren't fully in your control.
myth.why: You can decide wisely and still face an uncertain result.

scenarios.relearn: A good decision is made well, not one guaranteed to turn out perfectly.

scenarios.hook: You realise a past decision didn't work out.

options.text: Learn from it and adjust; that's deciding well over time
options.consequence: You grow your judgement instead of freezing.

options.text: Decide you're bad at decisions and give up
options.consequence: One choice that didn't work is data to learn from, not proof you 'can't decide'.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding well includes learning from the ones that don't pan out.
scenarios.relearn: Learn from a decision that didn't work; that's deciding well over time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which part of deciding do you most want to get better at?
scenarios.affirm: Strengthening any one of those makes your decisions wiser and more yours.
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values, long-term thinking and resisting pressure are all parts of deciding well.

scenarios.hook: A choice is genuinely hard and both options have real costs.

options.text: Accept that hard trade-offs are normal, and choose by your priorities
options.consequence: You decide with clear eyes, not paralysis.

options.text: Avoid deciding and let it happen to you
options.consequence: Hard trade-offs are normal; choose by your priorities rather than avoiding.

scenarios.debrief: Some decisions have no painless option; your priorities break the tie.
scenarios.relearn: For hard trade-offs, decide by your priorities; avoiding is still a choice.

scenarios.hook: Spot the pressure that shouldn't drive a big decision.

scene.text: A clear look at your own goals

scenarios.why: 'Everyone's doing it' and false urgency are pressure; your own goals aren't.
scenarios.relearn: Spot pressure like 'everyone's doing it' and false urgency in big decisions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: deciding by your own values, within safety and the law, is real adult freedom. Feel it?
scenarios.affirm: Within safety and law, deciding by your own values is exactly what adult freedom is.
scenarios.relearn: Deciding by your own values, within safety and law, is adult freedom.

scenarios.hook: "Feeling stressed about exams means you're weak or not coping."

myth.un: Exam stress means you're weak or failing to cope.
myth.re: Stress at big moments is normal; tools and support help you handle it.
myth.why: Around 81% of students feel exam anxiety, you're far from alone.

scenarios.relearn: Exam stress is normal, not weakness; tools and support help.

scenarios.hook: Board exams are looming and the pressure feels huge.

options.text: Break it down, use a healthy routine, and lean on people
options.consequence: The mountain becomes manageable steps.

options.text: Panic and pull all-nighters on no sleep
options.consequence: Break it into steps and keep a healthy routine; panic and no sleep make it worse.

scenarios.debrief: Big stress shrinks when you break it down and keep healthy habits.
scenarios.relearn: For exam pressure: break it down, healthy routine, lean on people.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to handle stress, or a harmful one?
scenarios.relearn: Rest, movement and talking help; self-harm and bottling up don't.

scenarios.hook: "Your exam results decide your entire worth and future."

myth.un: Your results decide your whole worth and future.
myth.re: Results matter, but they don't define your worth, and there are many paths forward.
myth.why: One exam is a moment, not the measure of a person.

scenarios.relearn: Results matter but don't define your worth; many paths exist.

scenarios.hook: "Failing at something makes you a failure."

myth.un: Failing at something makes you a failure.
myth.re: Failure is an event to learn from, not who you are.
myth.why: Almost everyone who succeeds has failed along the way.

scenarios.relearn: Failure is an event to learn from, not your identity.

scenarios.hook: You're about to leave home for the first time and feel anxious.

options.text: Name it as a normal big change, prepare, and stay connected to your people
options.consequence: You meet the change supported, not alone.

options.text: Pretend you feel nothing about it
options.consequence: Big changes stir feelings; name them, prepare, and stay connected.

scenarios.debrief: Naming a big transition and staying connected makes it manageable.
scenarios.relearn: For a big change like leaving home: name it, prepare, stay connected.

scenarios.hook: The future feels uncertain and that's making you anxious.

options.text: Focus on the next right step you can control
options.consequence: Uncertainty shrinks to something you can act on.

options.text: Spiral over everything you can't control
options.consequence: Focus on the next controllable step; spiralling over the uncontrollable drains you.

scenarios.debrief: You can't control the future, but you can take the next right step.
scenarios.relearn: For uncertainty, focus on the next step you can control.

scenarios.hook: A relationship is ending or changing as you move on in life.

options.text: Allow the feelings, lean on support, and be kind to yourself
options.consequence: You grieve the change healthily and heal.

options.text: Suppress it and push through alone
options.consequence: Allow the feelings and lean on support; suppressing alone prolongs it.

scenarios.debrief: Changing relationships bring real feelings; healthy coping and support help.
scenarios.relearn: For a changing relationship: feel it, lean on support, be kind to yourself.

scenarios.hook: Your stress has become heavy and persistent, not just a hard week.

options.text: Reach real support, a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416
options.consequence: You get help before it overwhelms you.

options.text: Tell yourself to just push through
options.consequence: Persistent heavy stress deserves real support, a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.debrief: When stress is heavy and lasting, reaching for support is the wise move.
scenarios.relearn: For heavy, persistent stress, reach support like a trusted adult or 14416.

scenarios.hook: Match the 'handle the big stuff' step to what it does.
scenarios.relearn: Name it, break it down, and ask early, that's how you handle big stress.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it. Hear that?
scenarios.affirm: Change is genuinely hard for everyone; finding it hard is human, not failure.
scenarios.relearn: Change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the healthy response to a setback.

scene.text: Taking a breath and a small next step

scenarios.why: A breath, a small step, and asking for support are healthy; harsh self-blame isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Meet a setback with a small step and support, not self-blame.

scenarios.hook: You're carrying a lot and running on empty.

options.text: Build in rest and basics; you can't pour from empty
options.consequence: You recover the capacity to cope.

options.text: Keep going with no rest or food
options.consequence: Rest and the basics aren't optional; you can't run on empty for long.

scenarios.debrief: Rest, food and basic care are part of handling hard times, not a luxury.
scenarios.relearn: Build in rest and basics; you can't cope well on empty.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: adulthood has hard moments, and you can be equipped to meet them. Feel readier?
scenarios.affirm: Hard moments are part of adult life, and you're building the tools to meet them.
scenarios.relearn: Adulthood has hard moments; you can be equipped to meet them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you through a transition, or makes it harder?
scenarios.relearn: Preparing and leaning on support help; pretending and isolating make it harder.

scenarios.hook: "You should handle big stress completely on your own now."

myth.un: You should handle big stress entirely on your own now.
myth.re: Leaning on people is part of handling stress well, at any age.
myth.why: Support multiplies your capacity to cope.

scenarios.relearn: Handling stress well includes leaning on people, not doing it alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which 'big stuff' tool do you most want in your pocket?
scenarios.affirm: Carry that tool, it'll meet you in exactly the hard moment you'll need it.
scenarios.relearn: Breaking it down, routine, asking early and self-kindness handle the big stuff.

scenarios.hook: You need to communicate something difficult clearly.

yourLine.text: "Can we talk? Here's what's on my mind, honestly and calmly."
Hint at it and hope they guess

scenarios.relearn: Clear, calm, honest communication beats hinting and hoping.

scenarios.hook: Someone's talking and you want to really listen.

yourLine.text: "So what I'm hearing is... is that right?"
Plan your reply while they talk

scenarios.relearn: Reflecting back what you heard is real listening.

scenarios.hook: A group task needs everyone pulling together.

options.text: Share roles by strength and keep everyone included
options.consequence: The team works well together.

options.text: Take over and do it all yourself
options.consequence: Collaboration means shared roles and inclusion, not taking over.

scenarios.debrief: Good collaboration shares the load by strengths and includes everyone.
scenarios.relearn: Collaborate by sharing roles and including everyone.

scenarios.hook: You need to set a boundary with someone.

yourLine.text: "I'm not able to do that, but here's what I can do."

scenarios.relearn: A clear, respectful boundary beats a resentful yes.

scenarios.hook: A conflict with a friend is brewing.

options.text: Address it calmly, listen, and look for a fair resolution
options.consequence: The friendship comes through stronger.

options.text: Let it fester or blow up
options.consequence: Address conflict calmly and look for a fair resolution; festering or exploding hurts both.

scenarios.debrief: Conflict handled calmly and fairly can strengthen a relationship.
scenarios.relearn: Address conflict calmly, listen, and seek a fair resolution.

scenarios.hook: "Being good with people is just something you're born with."

myth.un: People skills are something you're just born with.
myth.re: Communication, listening, boundaries and conflict skills are all learnable.
myth.why: Like any skill, they grow with practice.

scenarios.relearn: People skills are learnable, not just innate.

scenarios.hook: Sort: strengthens a relationship, or strains it?
scenarios.relearn: Listening and respecting boundaries strengthen relationships; talking over and resentment strain them.

scenarios.hook: You'll soon work with people you didn't choose (college, a job).

options.text: Lead with respect and clear communication, even with people you clash with
options.consequence: You work well across differences.

options.text: Only cooperate with people you like
options.consequence: Adult life means working respectfully even with people you wouldn't choose.

scenarios.debrief: Working respectfully across differences is core to adult and work life.
scenarios.relearn: Work with respect and clear communication, even with people you clash with.

scenarios.hook: You disagree with someone but want to keep it respectful.

yourLine.text: "I see it differently, can I explain why, and hear your side?"

scenarios.relearn: Respectful disagreement explains and listens, rather than attacks.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: half of adult life is other people, so people skills are worth real practice. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Investing in people skills pays off in nearly every part of adult life.
scenarios.relearn: People skills are half of adult life and worth real practice.

scenarios.hook: Someone crosses a boundary you set.

options.text: Restate it calmly and hold it
options.consequence: Your boundary is taken seriously.

options.text: Drop it to avoid friction
options.consequence: Restate and hold a crossed boundary; dropping it teaches people to ignore it.

scenarios.debrief: A boundary only works if you hold it, calmly and consistently.
scenarios.relearn: If a boundary is crossed, restate it calmly and hold it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: emotional intelligence with others, or the opposite?
scenarios.relearn: Noticing feelings and clear communication are EQ; ignoring and assuming aren't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which people skill do you most want to grow?
scenarios.affirm: Growing that skill will improve your friendships, family and future work.
scenarios.relearn: Listening, boundaries, conflict and clear talk are people skills to grow.

scenarios.hook: You hurt someone unintentionally and they're upset.

options.text: Listen, take responsibility, and make it right
options.consequence: Trust is repaired.

options.text: Get defensive and minimise it
options.consequence: Listening and owning it repairs trust; defensiveness widens the rift.

scenarios.debrief: Owning your impact and repairing it is a mature people skill.
scenarios.relearn: If you hurt someone, listen, take responsibility, and make it right.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: being good with people isn't about being liked by all, it's about respect both ways. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Mutual respect, not universal popularity, is the heart of real people skills.
scenarios.relearn: People skills are about mutual respect, not being liked by everyone.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help means you've failed at being an adult."

myth.un: Asking for help means you've failed at adulting.
myth.re: Help-seeking is a lifelong strength; capable adults lean on people too.
myth.why: No one does adult life entirely alone.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for help is a lifelong strength, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who's in your support network, the people you can lean on?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing who you can lean on means you're never truly facing things alone.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your support network means you're never facing things alone.

scenarios.hook: "Once you turn 18 you stop needing support."

myth.un: Once you're 18 you stop needing support.
myth.re: Needing people never expires; help-seeking continues for life.
myth.why: Adults rely on networks throughout their lives.

scenarios.relearn: Needing support never expires; it continues for life.

scenarios.hook: Match the support to what it's good for.
scenarios.relearn: Different supports, friends, mentors, professionals, suit different needs.

scenarios.hook: You're struggling but feel you shouldn't 'burden' anyone.

options.text: Reach out anyway; real connections want to be there for you
options.consequence: You get support and the relationship deepens.

options.text: Keep it all to yourself
options.consequence: You're not a burden; real connections want to support you, reach out.

scenarios.debrief: Letting people support you isn't a burden; it's how connection works.
scenarios.relearn: Reach out when struggling; you're not a burden to people who care.

scenarios.hook: Your struggle is bigger than friends and family can help with.

options.text: Reach a professional or a helpline (Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN)
options.consequence: You get the right level of help.

options.text: Keep relying only on friends for something serious
options.consequence: For bigger struggles, reach a professional or a helpline like Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.debrief: Matching the help to the size of the struggle is wise self-care.
scenarios.relearn: For bigger struggles, reach a professional or Tele-MANAS 14416 / KIRAN.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: building your network before you need it means it's there when you do. See the value?
scenarios.affirm: A network built early is a safety net that's there the moment you need it.
scenarios.relearn: Build your support network before you need it.

scenarios.hook: You want to reach out to someone for support.

yourLine.text: "I'm going through something and could use someone to talk to, do you have time?"
Hint at it and hope they notice

scenarios.relearn: A simple, direct 'I could use someone to talk to' opens real support.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a support network, or isolates you?

items.text: Insisting on doing it all alone

scenarios.relearn: Staying in touch and asking early build support; cutting off and going solo isolate you.

scenarios.hook: A friend is struggling and reaches out to you.

options.text: Listen, support, and help them find help if it's big
options.consequence: You're a real part of their support network.

options.text: Brush them off, you're busy
options.consequence: Listening and helping them find help is being a real support, both ways.

scenarios.debrief: Support networks work both ways, being there for others too.
scenarios.relearn: Be a support for others: listen and help them find help if it's big.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: self-care habits, sleep, movement, downtime, keep you able to cope. Worth building now?
scenarios.affirm: Self-care habits built now will steady you through all of adult life.
scenarios.relearn: Self-care habits like sleep and downtime keep you able to cope.

scenarios.hook: "Reaching out for mental-health support is shameful."

myth.un: Reaching out for mental-health support is shameful.
myth.re: It's a normal, smart, strong thing to do, just like any other health care.
myth.why: Stigma is the only thing that makes it feel otherwise.

scenarios.relearn: Reaching out for mental-health support is normal, smart and strong.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'you don't have to do adulthood alone', does that land as a relief?
scenarios.affirm: You really don't have to do it alone, that's the most important message here.
scenarios.relearn: You don't have to do adulthood alone.

scenarios.hook: Match the toolkit part to what it gives you.
scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge, the decision method and stress tools are core toolkit parts.

scenarios.hook: Match the rest of the toolkit.
scenarios.relearn: People skills, your support network and self-care complete the toolkit.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the toolkit you've carried since you were small is now ready for adult life. Feel equipped?
scenarios.affirm: Everything you've built since the start is now a toolkit for your whole adult life.
scenarios.relearn: Your life-skills toolkit is now ready for adult life.

scenarios.hook: You want to actually use this, not just know it.

options.text: Pick one tool to put into practice this week
options.consequence: The toolkit becomes part of how you live.

options.text: Leave it as 'nice to know'
options.consequence: Put one tool into practice this week; that's how it becomes real.

scenarios.debrief: A tool used once becomes a habit you keep.
scenarios.relearn: Put one tool into practice this week to make it real.

scenarios.hook: Sort: in your Life-Ready toolkit, or not?

scenarios.hook: Lensy: being 'life ready' isn't having it all figured out, it's having the tools and your people. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Life-ready means equipped and supported, not having every answer, and you are.
scenarios.relearn: Being life-ready is having the tools and your people, not all the answers.

scenarios.hook: A friend is anxious about 'adulting' and feeling alone in it.

options.text: Share the toolkit and remind them they're not alone

options.text: Tell them to just figure it out

scenarios.debrief: Passing on the toolkit and reassurance is real support.
scenarios.relearn: Share the toolkit and remind a friend they're not alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: biggest take-away from Life Ready?

scenarios.affirm: From a small friend naming feelings to a near-adult ready for life, that's real growth.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: whatever the future holds, you have a toolkit and people, and that's enough to start. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: A toolkit and your people is genuinely enough to step into adulthood, you're ready.
scenarios.relearn: A toolkit and your people is enough to step into adulthood.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: stepping into adult life equipped and not alone, worth carrying that forward?
